lines.name: Level: B2 · Topic: The Police Station

lines.text:
Order and Investigation — Inside a Police Station

A police station is where public safety is organised. It is simultaneously a workplace, an emergency coordination centre, and a point of contact between citizens and the law. Understanding how a police station operates — and the vocabulary that surrounds it — is essential for anyone living in or visiting an English-speaking country.

The building is divided by function. The front desk is where the public interacts with officers — filing reports, asking questions, or collecting documents. Behind it, the dispatch center coordinates emergency calls: a dispatcher receives reports and directs patrol officers to incidents via radio. A break room provides rest. A locker room stores personal equipment. A training room hosts ongoing education. A parking lot houses the fleet.

The investigative spaces are restricted. An interrogation room — a small, windowless room with a table and chairs — is where detectives question suspects. An evidence room stores physical items connected to cases: an evidence bag, a fingerprint, a mugshot, a case file. A holding cell temporarily detains arrested individuals before they are transferred or released. An armory secures weapons and tactical equipment.

Officers carry specialised equipment. A badge identifies rank and authority. Handcuffs restrain suspects. A radio maintains communication with dispatch and other units. A flashlight illuminates dark areas. A baton is a striking tool used in close encounters. A body camera records interactions — increasingly required by policy. A vest provides ballistic protection. A taser and pepper spray are non-lethal alternatives. A whistle directs traffic or signals for attention.

Ranks structure the chain of command. A patrol officer is the most visible — driving a patrol car, walking a beat, responding to calls. A sergeant supervises a team of officers. A detective investigates crimes after they occur, working from a desk rather than a patrol car. A traffic officer manages road safety — enforcing the speed limit, monitoring traffic lights and crosswalks, setting up cones and barriers, and placing caution tape at accident scenes. A K9 officer works with a trained dog — the K9 unit — to detect drugs, explosives, or missing persons. An undercover officer works without a uniform, often using an undercover car. A forensic analyst examines physical evidence — fingerprints, DNA, fibres. A chief leads the entire station.

The vehicle fleet includes patrol cars, motorcycles, SUVs, vans, bicycles, boats (in waterfront districts), and occasionally a helicopter for aerial support. Each has a siren, a camera, and communications equipment. An ambulance is called when injuries occur.

Legal documents govern the work. A report documents an incident. A warrant authorises a search or an arrest. An ID card confirms an officer's identity. A notebook and a pen record observations. A computer stores digital records.

Traffic management is a daily responsibility. A stop sign, a traffic light, a crosswalk, a speed limit sign, a barrier, a cone, and caution tape are the tools of road safety. A camera captures violations. An alarm signals a security breach.

Policing is complex, often contested, and always evolving — but the vocabulary is concrete and immediately useful.

lines.text: Scene: A person reporting a stolen bicycle at the police station
lines.name: Scene: A person reporting a stolen bicycle at the police station

lines.text: Good afternoon. How can I help you?
lines.name: Good afternoon. How can I help you?

lines.text: I'd like to report a theft. My bicycle was stolen.
lines.name: I'd like to report a theft. My bicycle was stolen.

lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. When and where did this happen?
lines.name: I'm sorry to hear that. When and where did this happen?

lines.text: It was outside the library on Park Road. I locked it at about 2pm and when I came back at 4pm, it was gone.
lines.name: It was outside the library on Park Road. I locked it at about 2pm and when I came back at 4pm, it was gone.

lines.text: Was it locked with a chain or a D-lock?
lines.name: Was it locked with a chain or a D-lock?

lines.text: A chain lock. The chain was cut and left on the ground.
lines.name: A chain lock. The chain was cut and left on the ground.

lines.text: Can you describe the bicycle? Make, model, colour?
lines.name: Can you describe the bicycle? Make, model, colour?

lines.text: It's a blue Trek mountain bike, about two years old. I have the serial number at home.
lines.name: It's a blue Trek mountain bike, about two years old. I have the serial number at home.

lines.text: Good — please send us the serial number. Is there any CCTV in that area?

lines.text: I think the library might have cameras outside.
lines.name: I think the library might have cameras outside.

lines.text: We'll check. I'll give you a crime reference number. You'll need it for your insurance claim.

lines.text: Will you be able to find it?

lines.text: We'll do our best. Many stolen bikes turn up for sale online — keep an eye on local selling sites.

lines.text: 'Police' is a plural noun — always takes a plural verb: 'The police are', 'The police have.' Never *'the police is.' For singular reference, use 'a police officer', 'a detective', or 'a member of the police force.' Similar collective plurals: 'people are' (not *people is), 'staff are' (British English).

lines.text: 'Tell' + direct object (no 'to'): 'told the suspect.' 'Say' + 'to': 'said to the suspect.' Never *'told to the suspect.' Pattern: 'The detective told him that...' / 'The detective said to him that...' / 'The detective said that...' The person after 'tell' is always a direct object without a preposition.

Pattern: 'The detective told him that...' / 'The detective said to him that...' / 'The detective said that...' The person after 'tell' is always a direct object without a preposition.

lines.text: ❌ "The officer suggested the witness to describe what she had seen at the crosswalk."
lines.name: ❌ "The officer suggested the witness to describe what she had seen at the crosswalk."

lines.text: ✅ "The officer suggested that the witness describe what she had seen at the crosswalk."
lines.name: ✅ "The officer suggested that the witness describe what she had seen at the crosswalk."

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggest someone to do). Use: suggest + that-clause (subjunctive): 'suggested that she describe.' Suggest + gerund: 'suggested describing.' Same restriction: 'recommend', 'propose.' Compare: 'The officer asked the witness to describe...' — 'ask' DOES take object + infinitive.

lines.text: ✅ "A patrol car had been parked in front of the station since early morning." / "A patrol car was parked in front of the station from early morning."

lines.text: 'Since' requires a perfect tense: 'has been parked since...' (present perfect — still there) or 'had been parked since...' (past perfect — before another past event). Past simple with 'since' is incorrect. 'From' can replace 'since' with past simple: 'was parked from early morning.' Choose the tense that matches the time frame.

lines.text: ❌ "There are less crimes in this neighbourhood compared to five years ago."
lines.name: ❌ "There are less crimes in this neighbourhood compared to five years ago."

lines.text: ✅ "There are fewer crimes in this neighbourhood compared to five years ago."
lines.name: ✅ "There are fewer crimes in this neighbourhood compared to five years ago."

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer crimes', 'fewer incidents', 'fewer arrests.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less crime' (uncountable general concept), 'less violence', 'less corruption.' Note: 'crime' can be countable (specific offences: 'three crimes') or uncountable (the general phenomenon: 'crime is rising'). Choose fewer/less based on how the noun is used in context.

lines.text: UK: 999 (emergency) or 101 (non-emergency police). US: 911. EU: 112 (works across Europe, also works in the UK). Use 999/911 for emergencies only — life in danger, crime in progress. Use 101 for non-urgent matters like reporting minor crimes after the fact.

lines.text: UK: Police Constable → Sergeant → Inspector → Chief Inspector → Superintendent → Chief Constable. US: Officer → Sergeant → Lieutenant → Captain → Chief of Police. UK police generally do not carry firearms (except specialist armed units). US police routinely carry firearms.

lines.text: 'Rob' = steal from a person or place using threat/force: 'He was robbed at knifepoint.' 'Steal' = take something: 'Someone stole my phone.' 'Burgle' (BrE) / 'burglarize' (AmE) = break into a building to steal: 'Our house was burgled.' 'Mug' = rob someone in a public place.
lines.name: 'Rob' = steal from a person or place using threat/force: 'He was robbed at knifepoint.' 'Steal' = take something: 'Someone stole my phone.' 'Burgle' (BrE) / 'burglarize' (AmE) = break into a building to steal: 'Our house was burgled.' 'Mug' = rob someone in a public place.

lines.text: 'Lawyer' = general term (both BrE and AmE). 'Solicitor' (BrE) = a lawyer who advises clients and handles legal documents. 'Barrister' (BrE) = a lawyer who speaks in court. 'Attorney' (AmE) = the main American term for lawyer. In the US, one lawyer does both roles.
